input.content:
## Destination

The multi-tenant fork of Headscale (**P0-2**, #2) is decided end-to-end — every hard-to-reverse choice for *cutting the fork* and *reshaping Headscale's data model* into Org→Tailnet→User→Node with row-level `tenant_id` (never null, N=1 self-host) is locked, so #2 can be executed without further decisions. Output: ADRs + spec updates ready to hand off.

## Notes

- Domain: Headscale fork → multi-tenant Tailscale control plane. The **schema shape is already locked** (wiki [Architecture](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/wiki/Architecture), 8 decisions; datastore = libSQL single-node, ADR-0005). This map charts **how to realize that shape in Headscale's actual code**, not what the shape is.
- Skills every session: `/grilling` + `/domain-modeling`. Tracker: GitHub (`docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`).
- **Planning only** — produce decisions/ADRs, not fork code. Writing the fork is execution, handed to #2 once the way is clear.
- Wiki's in-repo source-of-truth links (`CONTEXT.md`, `docs/adr/`, `BUILD_ORDER.md`) are currently **dead** — those decisions live only in the wiki. Reconciling them into real files is a separate effort, not this map.
- Research findings live on `research/*` branches (linked per closed ticket below), not on `main`.
- **Fork stance locked (#30): maintained fork, module path `github.com/juanfont/headscale` unchanged** — all divergence decisions below assume upstream merges must stay low-conflict.

## Decisions so far

<!-- one line per closed ticket -->

- [Fork map: Headscale data model + single-tailnet scope](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/26) — Headscale is single-tenant by construction: one global `IPAllocator` singleton, 3 UNIQUE username indexes, a single ACL-policy row, one MagicDNS `base_domain`. Multi-tailnet = new `tenants`/`tailnets` tables + non-null `tenant_id`/`tailnet_id` on users/nodes/keys/policies, and re-scope IP allocation, user uniqueness, policy loading, DNS suffix. → `research/headscale-data-model`.
- [Fork map: IP allocation → per-Tailnet /10](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/27) — one server-wide `IPAllocator` singleton (`hscontrol/db/ip.go`), in-memory `usedIPs` seeded from ALL nodes (no tenant filter), no DB unique constraint on IPs. Per-Tailnet = add `TenantID` + `UNIQUE(tenant_id, ipv4/ipv6)`, de-singleton allocator with tenant-filtered seed, thread tenant through `Next()`/`FreeIPs`/`BackfillNodeIPs`; `100.64.0.0/10` stays shared config. → `research/headscale-ip-allocation`.
- [Fork map: registration + pre-auth key flow](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/28) — single authenticated `POST /register` (machine identity = Noise-session MachineKey, never URL) dispatches auth-key vs OIDC; pre-auth keys bcrypt-hashed. Node→tenant binding at exactly two chokepoints (`state.go:2807` auth-key path, `state.go:2205` OIDC path). Tenant-scope = add `TenantID` to PreAuthKey/User/Node, stamp from the credential (decision #4). → `research/headscale-registration`.
- [Fork map: GORM dialect + migrations on libSQL](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/29) — two-dialect GORM (glebarez pure-Go SQLite / Postgres) + `go-gormigrate` versioned migrations run at startup; libSQL works via the SQLite driver. No RLS anywhere → tenant scoping AND node-pubkey uniqueness are **app-layer only** (no DB unique index to lean on). → `research/headscale-gorm-migrations`.
- [Decision: fork strategy](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/30) — **maintained fork**, not hard fork. Go module path stays `github.com/juanfont/headscale` (merges stay low-conflict); new identity is **brand-layer only** (repo/CLI/Docker/config/product name, never `go.mod`). Upstream tracked via a live `upstream` remote + scheduled CI (fetch → merge → P0-4 harness; green auto-PR, conflict/red human-resolves). P0-4 harness doubles as the upstream-sync merge gate. Ceiling: automation is best-effort + harness-gated, not conflict-free.

## Not yet specified

- ADR authoring for the locked fork decisions — graduates once the remaining decision tickets (#31–#33) resolve; batch into ADRs then (fork-strategy #30 is the first candidate).
- Scoped-repository concrete API + CI-guard implementation — graduates once #31's direction is set (likely a prototype ticket). Research confirms no RLS, so enforcement is entirely in code.
- Upstream-sync CI job (scheduled fetch → merge → harness → auto-PR) — design likely lives in **P0-4 (#4) / P0-5 (#5)** execution, not this map; flagged here so it isn't lost.
- Compat-harness (#4, P0-4) handoff — what "builds green" + protocol-drift signal P0-2 must expose to the harness (now also the merge gate).

## Out of scope

- Writing the actual fork / migration code — execution, handed to #2 after this map clears.
- Datastore engine choice — resolved (libSQL single-node, ADR-0005).
- Phase 1+ features (#6–#21).

content.text:
Claimed **#31** (scoped-repo + CI guard). Grilling.

---

## The crux — #30 already narrows this hard

No RLS (research #29) → scoping is 100% in code. But **#30 (maintained fork)** is the real constraint: upstream Headscale does `db.Where(...)` on `User`/`Node`/`PreAuthKey` in hundreds of unscoped call sites (`state.go`, `db/*.go`). Two mechanisms, and merge-friendliness splits them violently:

**(a) Scoped GORM session + auto-injecting callback.** Bind `tenant_id` to the `*gorm.DB` **in context**; a global `BeforeQuery`/`BeforeUpdate`/`BeforeDelete` callback auto-adds `WHERE tenant_id = ?` to any tenant-table query. Upstream's existing `db.Where(...)` calls **inherit scope for free** — you don't rewrite call sites, so upstream merges stay clean (honors #30). The scoping lives at one seam.

**(b) Explicit repository layer / interface.** All tenant-table access routes through a hand-written repo; raw `db` banned. Stronger *compile-time* story, but you must **rewrite every upstream call site** to go through the repo → every upstream merge is a war. **Fights #30.**

Given #30, (a) is strongly favored. But (a) has sharp edges you must rule on.

## Three questions

**Q1 — mechanism.** (a) auto-scoping GORM session, or (b) explicit repo layer? I read #30 as forcing **(a)**. Fight me if you want the compile-time guarantees of (b) badly enough to pay the merge tax.

**Q2 — fail-closed + escape hatch.** With (a): if a query runs with **no `tenant_id` in context**, it must **error** (fail closed), never silently return all tenants' rows. Agree? And legit cross-tenant ops exist — `IPAllocator` seed (reads all nodes), admin/ops, the N=1 migration (#32). Those need an **explicit, greppable escape hatch** (e.g. `db.Unscoped()`-style `WithAllTenants(ctx)`). Confirm the fail-closed stance + that cross-tenant access must be explicit, not default.

**Q3 — what fails the build.** The CI guard. Options:
- **Type-level** — root `*gorm.DB` handle is unexported; only the context-scoped accessor is exported from the db package. Compiler enforces; nothing to lint. Cleanest, but constrains how upstream code reaches the handle.
- **Linter** — custom `go/analysis` vet pass (or `ruleguard`/`semgrep`) failing CI on raw-root-handle use outside the db package + on un-reviewed escape-hatch calls.
- Both: type-level for the handle, linter for escape-hatch audit.

Which guard? And does the guard run **only on RavenScale-authored packages**, or the whole tree including merged-upstream files (which will trip it until refactored)?

Answer Q1–Q3. I'll push the fuzzy ones, then lock #31.

content.text:
Q1 **(a)**, Q2/Q3 = my recommendations. Locking with the design calls I flagged.

## Decision — #31

**Mechanism (a): context-scoped GORM session + global auto-injecting callback.**
- `tenant_id` bound to request context at the **auth seam** (middleware reads the trusted tenant claim / pre-auth-key tenant — the `state.go` chokepoints from #28). `TenantDB(ctx)` returns a `*gorm.DB` carrying the tenant + a registered `BeforeQuery/Update/Delete` callback that appends `WHERE tenant_id = ?` to tenant-table statements. Upstream `db.Where(...)` call sites **inherit scope for free** → merge-friendly (#30).
- **Fail closed:** tenant-table op with no `tenant_id` in context → callback **errors**, never returns cross-tenant rows.
- **Escape hatch:** explicit + greppable `WithAllTenants(ctx)` for the legit few — `IPAllocator` seed (#27), admin/ops, N=1 migration (#32). Cross-tenant is opt-in, never default.
- **CI guard:** custom `go/analysis` vet pass fails the build on (1) raw root-handle use outside the sanctioned `db` package, (2) un-annotated escape-hatch calls. Full type-level unexporting **deferred** — it fights upstream's direct handle use; funnel + lint instead. Runs whole-tree, `db` package allowlisted; a new raw-root access from an upstream merge trips the guard → resolved at merge (consistent with #30's harness-gated sync).

**Open risk → graduate a prototype:** GORM callbacks may miss `Preload`, joins, or raw SQL — need to prove auto-scope + fail-closed + escape hatch hold across Headscale's real query shapes before handoff.

Recording, closing, graduating the prototype.

## Destination

The multi-tenant fork of Headscale (**P0-2**, #2) is decided end-to-end — every hard-to-reverse choice for *cutting the fork* and *reshaping Headscale's data model* into Org→Tailnet→User→Node with row-level `tenant_id` (never null, N=1 self-host) is locked, so #2 can be executed without further decisions. Output: ADRs + spec updates ready to hand off.

## Notes

- Domain: Headscale fork → multi-tenant Tailscale control plane. The **schema shape is already locked** (wiki [Architecture](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/wiki/Architecture), 8 decisions; datastore = libSQL single-node, ADR-0005). This map charts **how to realize that shape in Headscale's actual code**, not what the shape is.
- Skills every session: `/grilling` + `/domain-modeling`. Tracker: GitHub (`docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`).
- **Planning only** — produce decisions/ADRs, not fork code. Writing the fork is execution, handed to #2 once the way is clear.
- Wiki's in-repo source-of-truth links (`CONTEXT.md`, `docs/adr/`, `BUILD_ORDER.md`) are currently **dead** — those decisions live only in the wiki. Reconciling them into real files is a separate effort, not this map.
- Research findings live on `research/*` branches (linked per closed ticket below), not on `main`.
- **Fork stance locked (#30): maintained fork, module path `github.com/juanfont/headscale` unchanged** — all divergence decisions below assume upstream merges must stay low-conflict.
- **Scoping mechanism locked (#31): auto-scoping GORM session** (context-bound `tenant_id` + callback) — chosen precisely so upstream call sites inherit scope without rewrites.

## Decisions so far

<!-- one line per closed ticket -->

- [Fork map: Headscale data model + single-tailnet scope](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/26) — Headscale is single-tenant by construction: one global `IPAllocator` singleton, 3 UNIQUE username indexes, a single ACL-policy row, one MagicDNS `base_domain`. Multi-tailnet = new `tenants`/`tailnets` tables + non-null `tenant_id`/`tailnet_id` on users/nodes/keys/policies, and re-scope IP allocation, user uniqueness, policy loading, DNS suffix. → `research/headscale-data-model`.
- [Fork map: IP allocation → per-Tailnet /10](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/27) — one server-wide `IPAllocator` singleton (`hscontrol/db/ip.go`), in-memory `usedIPs` seeded from ALL nodes (no tenant filter), no DB unique constraint on IPs. Per-Tailnet = add `TenantID` + `UNIQUE(tenant_id, ipv4/ipv6)`, de-singleton allocator with tenant-filtered seed, thread tenant through `Next()`/`FreeIPs`/`BackfillNodeIPs`; `100.64.0.0/10` stays shared config. → `research/headscale-ip-allocation`.
- [Fork map: registration + pre-auth key flow](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/28) — single authenticated `POST /register` (machine identity = Noise-session MachineKey, never URL) dispatches auth-key vs OIDC; pre-auth keys bcrypt-hashed. Node→tenant binding at exactly two chokepoints (`state.go:2807` auth-key path, `state.go:2205` OIDC path). Tenant-scope = add `TenantID` to PreAuthKey/User/Node, stamp from the credential (decision #4). → `research/headscale-registration`.
- [Fork map: GORM dialect + migrations on libSQL](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/29) — two-dialect GORM (glebarez pure-Go SQLite / Postgres) + `go-gormigrate` versioned migrations run at startup; libSQL works via the SQLite driver. No RLS anywhere → tenant scoping AND node-pubkey uniqueness are **app-layer only** (no DB unique index to lean on). → `research/headscale-gorm-migrations`.
- [Decision: fork strategy](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/30) — **maintained fork**, not hard fork. Go module path stays `github.com/juanfont/headscale` (merges stay low-conflict); new identity is **brand-layer only** (repo/CLI/Docker/config/product name, never `go.mod`). Upstream tracked via a live `upstream` remote + scheduled CI (fetch → merge → P0-4 harness; green auto-PR, conflict/red human-resolves). P0-4 harness doubles as the upstream-sync merge gate. Ceiling: automation is best-effort + harness-gated, not conflict-free.
- [Decision: scoped-repository + CI guard](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/31) — **auto-scoping GORM session**: `tenant_id` bound to request context at the auth seam (#28 chokepoints); `TenantDB(ctx)` + `BeforeQuery/Update/Delete` callback injects `WHERE tenant_id = ?`, so upstream call sites inherit scope without rewrites (honors #30). **Fail-closed** (no tenant → error, never all-rows). Explicit greppable `WithAllTenants(ctx)` escape hatch for the legit few (IPAllocator seed, admin, N=1 migration). CI guard = custom `go/analysis` vet pass (fails on raw-root-handle use outside the `db` package + un-annotated escape-hatch calls); type-level unexporting deferred. Residual risk → prototype #34.

## Not yet specified

- ADR authoring for the locked fork decisions — graduates once the remaining decision tickets (#32–#33) resolve; batch into ADRs then (#30, #31 already candidates).
- Upstream-sync CI job (scheduled fetch → merge → harness → auto-PR) — design likely lives in **P0-4 (#4) / P0-5 (#5)** execution, not this map; flagged here so it isn't lost.
- Compat-harness (#4, P0-4) handoff — what "builds green" + protocol-drift signal P0-2 must expose to the harness (now also the merge gate).

## Out of scope

- Writing the actual fork / migration code — execution, handed to #2 after this map clears.
- Datastore engine choice — resolved (libSQL single-node, ADR-0005).
- Phase 1+ features (#6–#21).

content.text:
Claimed **#32** (N=1 migration). Grilling — and there's a scope question underneath this one that changes everything.

---

## The crux: is there anything to *backfill*?

Decision #5 / the wiki say "backfill `tenant_id` on every existing row." But **backfill only exists if untenanted rows exist**. RavenScale is greenfield and multi-tenant from P0-2 — the *first* real schema. Every RavenScale row is **born with `tenant_id`** (stamped at the #28 chokepoints, scoped by #31). So who has null-tenant rows to backfill?

Only two sources:
- **(A) Importing a real `juanfont/headscale` deployment** — someone points RavenScale at an existing single-tailnet Headscale DB and it upgrades in place. *That's* the backfill case.
- **(B)** A pre-tenancy RavenScale instance — doesn't exist; tenancy lands in the first schema.

So the whole shape of #32 forks on one question:

**Do we promise "existing Headscale DB → RavenScale, in place"?**
- **Yes** → #32 is a real **backfill migration**: create default Org+Tailnet, stamp `tenant_id`/`tailnet_id` on every legacy user/node/key/policy, re-key IP allocations (#27) under the default Tailnet. Strong compat promise, real risk.
- **No (greenfield only)** → #32 collapses to a **seed**: first boot ensures a default Org + default Tailnet; every insert is tenanted from birth. No backfill, tiny surface. The "migration" is just idempotent seed data.

Given Phase 0 has **zero existing deployments**, I lean **No — seed only**, and rule Headscale-DB import **out of scope** (revisit if a real migrating customer appears).

## Questions

**Q1 — the fork above.** Seed-only (greenfield, my rec) or full backfill (support Headscale-DB import now)? This is the decision; everything else follows.

**Q2 — migration ordering vs upstream (#30).** Our tenant schema + seed migrations live in the go-gormigrate slice alongside upstream's. gormigrate runs in **slice order**, and upstream merges insert their migrations into that slice → ordering/ID-collision friction. Namespace our migration IDs (e.g. `rs-0001-tenancy`) and pin them to run **after** upstream's schema migrations? Or accept manual ordering at each merge?

**Q3 — idempotency + rollback stance.** One-way (no down migration, per wiki), wrapped in a transaction, re-runnable safe, fail-closed (no partial state that leaves visible null-tenant rows). Confirm — or do you want a reversible path?

Answer Q1 first (it reshapes the rest). Push back if seed-only feels wrong.

content.text:
Claimed **#33** — the last decision. And grilling it surfaces a real collision with the wiki.

---

## The reframe: within-Tailnet uniqueness is a promise the *client* can't keep

Research says two things that matter here:
- #29: node pubkey uniqueness in Headscale is **app-enforced** (lookup-before-insert), and the node is identified by its **MachineKey** in the Noise handshake.
- #28: the Noise handshake authenticates the **MachineKey first** — *before* any pre-auth key / OIDC credential (which is where the Tailnet comes from).

So the **known-node reconnect lookup runs by MachineKey alone, pre-credential** (server decides "known node, refresh" vs "new, needs auth"). That lookup returns one node **only if MachineKey is globally unique.**

Wiki decision **#8 says "pubkey unique *within* a Tailnet."** But if a MachineKey could appear in two Tailnets, the reconnect lookup is **ambiguous** — and to disambiguate you'd need the client to send its Tailnet on reconnect. **The official Tailscale client sends no Tailnet selector** — it identifies by MachineKey, period. Operating principle #3: Tailscale owns that client, we can't change it.

**Therefore: cross-Tailnet same-device isn't merely "out of Phase-1 scope" (as #8 frames it) — it's client-blocked.** Composite-unique `(tailnet_id, machine_key)` *now* writes a schema that permits rows the reconnect path physically can't tell apart → a latent bug. It's actually a **Phase-3 client-fork trigger candidate** (a feature needing a client change), not a data-model choice.

## Recommendation
**Keep MachineKey globally unique for Phase 1.** Add `tenant_id`/`tailnet_id` columns (per #26 — future-proof, all queries scope), but the **uniqueness constraint stays global**. Everything else (peer lists, mapresponse, policy) is Tailnet-scoped via #31's auto-scope. Log cross-Tailnet-same-device as a client-fork trigger → route to **P3-1 (#20)**.

## Questions

**Q1 — constraint.** Global-unique MachineKey now (my rec), or composite `(tailnet_id, machine_key)`? I'm arguing composite-now is a latent bug the client can't back.

**Q2 — this contradicts wiki #8.** Per the "flag ADR conflicts" rule I'm surfacing it, not silently overriding. Accept **reopening #8**: schema carries the tenant columns, constraint stays **global** for Phase 1, cross-Tailnet device becomes a documented **P3 client-fork trigger** on #20? Or do you want to hold #8 as written and eat the latent-bug risk?

**Q3 — lookup paths.** One deliberate **global** lookup survives: the pre-credential known-node MachineKey lookup in the Noise handshake. Everything downstream (peer list, mapresponse, node-by-id) is tenant-scoped by #31. Confirm that split.

Answer Q1–Q3. Push hard on Q2 — it edits a "locked" decision.

Idempotent first-boot migration seeds a default Org + default Tailnet at fixed IDs (Org 1 / Tailnet 1); self-host and SaaS run the identical seed → single code path. - [Decision: node MachineKey uniqueness](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/33) — **MachineKey stays GLOBALLY unique in Phase 1**, not composited to `(tailnet_id, machine_key)`. # ADR-0006: Maintained fork of Headscale, not a hard fork

Status: Accepted (2026-08-12) · Decides [#30](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/30) · Map [#25](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/25)

## Context

RavenScale forks `juanfont/headscale` to add multi-tenancy. The tenant changes
are invasive (new tables, `tenant_id`/`tailnet_id` columns, a de-singletoned IP
allocator, tenant stamping inside `state.go`). Headscale ships upstream security
and protocol fixes on its own cadence, and P0-4 maintains a client-compat
harness. We must decide how much of upstream we keep receiving.

## Decision

Maintain an **upstream-tracking fork**, not a hard fork.

- **Go module path stays `github.com/juanfont/headscale`.** Imports are untouched
  so `git merge upstream/main` stays low-conflict. A module-path rename was
  rejected: it rewrites the import line in every `.go` file and turns every
  upstream sync into an all-files conflict.
- **New identity is brand-layer only** — repo name, CLI binary, Docker image,
  config keys, user-facing product name. None of these touch `go.mod`.
- **Upstream tracked** via a live `upstream` remote. A scheduled CI job fetches
  upstream, attempts the merge, and runs the P0-4 compat harness: green → auto-PR
  for review; conflict or red → a human resolves.
- **P0-4 harness doubles as the upstream-sync merge gate**, in addition to its
  Phase-2 role.

## Consequences

- Upstream security/protocol fixes flow in with modest effort; the invasive
  tenant surface will conflict whenever upstream edits those files, and those
  conflicts are resolved at merge time behind the harness gate.
- Fully-hands-off auto-merge is explicitly **not** a goal — automation is
  best-effort and harness-gated (the accepted ceiling).
- Publishing under an org-owned module path and "owning the tree" are given up
  for Phase 0–1; revisit only if divergence grows so large that tracking upstream
  stops paying off (that would be a fresh decision, effectively a hard fork).

# ADR-0007: Tenant scoping via an auto-scoping GORM session + CI guard

Status: Accepted (2026-08-12) · Decides [#31](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/31), validated by [#34](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/34) · Map [#25](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/25)

## Context

Isolation is row-level on shared infrastructure (ADR-0001). The datastore is
libSQL/SQLite (ADR-0005), which has **no row-level security** — so tenant
scoping must be guaranteed entirely in application code. ADR-0006 (maintained
fork) requires that whatever we choose does not force rewrites of upstream's
hundreds of unscoped `db.Where(...)` call sites, or every upstream merge becomes
a war.

## Decision

Enforce scoping with a **context-scoped GORM session and a global auto-injecting
callback**, not a hand-written repository layer.

- `tenant_id` is bound into the request `context` at the auth seam — from the
  trusted OIDC tenant claim or the pre-auth key's tenant (the two chokepoints in
  Headscale's registration flow). A `TenantDB(ctx)` accessor returns a `*gorm.DB`
  whose registered `BeforeQuery`/`BeforeUpdate`/`BeforeDelete` callback appends
  `WHERE tenant_id = ?` to any tenant-table statement. Upstream call sites inherit
  scope without modification.
- **Fail-closed**: a tenant-table operation with no `tenant_id` in context
  **errors**; it never returns all tenants' rows.
- **Explicit escape hatch**: legitimate cross-tenant/no-tenant operations
  (IP-allocator seed, admin/ops, the N=1 seed) go through a greppable
  `WithAllTenants(ctx)`. Cross-tenant access is opt-in and auditable.
- **CI guard**: a custom `go/analysis` vet pass fails the build on (1) raw
  root-handle use outside the sanctioned `db` package and (2) un-annotated
  `WithAllTenants` calls. Full type-level unexporting of the root handle is
  deferred (it fights upstream's direct handle use).

## Coverage and the two guard gaps (validated in #34)

Prototype `proto/gorm-tenant-scope` confirmed the callback scopes `Find`/`First`
and — importantly — **`Preload`** (which runs as a separate query through the
same callbacks). It does **not** cover two shapes, so the CI guard must also fail
the build (unless annotated / `WithAllTenants`) on:

- `.Raw(` / `.Exec(` touching a tenant table (bypasses the statement builder), and
- `.Joins(` whose joined table carries `tenant_id` without an explicit
  `<joined>.tenant_id = ?` predicate (only the primary table is auto-scoped).

## Consequences

- Upstream merges stay clean (ADR-0006 honored) because scoping lives at one seam.
- Correctness rests on `tenant_id` always being in context on request paths and on
  the CI guard catching the raw-SQL and join gaps; both are enforced in code/CI,
  not the DB.
- Every request path must carry a tenant-bound context; background jobs and
  migrations must use `WithAllTenants` deliberately.

# ADR-0008: N=1 self-host is a seed, not a backfill

Status: Accepted (2026-08-12) · Decides [#32](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/32) · Refines ADR-0003 · Map [#25](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/25)

## Context

ADR-0003 makes self-host simply N=1 (a default Org + Tailnet, `tenant_id` never
null) so there is a single code path. Decision #5 originally described this as
"backfill `tenant_id` on every existing row." But RavenScale is greenfield and
multi-tenant from the first real schema (P0-2): every row is born with a
`tenant_id` stamped at the auth chokepoints (ADR-0007). Untenanted rows only
exist if we import a pre-existing single-tailnet Headscale deployment.

## Decision

Treat N=1 as an **idempotent first-boot seed**, not a data backfill.

- A migration seeds a **default Org + default Tailnet at fixed IDs** (Org 1 /
  Tailnet 1). Self-host (N=1) and multi-tenant SaaS run the **identical** seed —
  there is no separate single-tenant mode and no `if single_tenant` branch.
- RavenScale migrations are namespaced `rs-NNNN-<name>` in the `go-gormigrate`
  slice and pinned to run **after** upstream's schema migrations (gormigrate runs
  in slice order); each upstream merge keeps the `rs-*` block appended after
  theirs.
- **One-way** (no down function), each migration transaction-wrapped and
  re-runnable safe (seed via `FirstOrCreate`). **Fail-closed**: the default
  Org+Tailnet row is guaranteed before any `tenant_id NOT NULL` column is added,
  and the migration aborts its transaction on any row it cannot tenant.
- Cross-tenant/no-tenant migration work runs through `WithAllTenants(ctx)`
  (ADR-0007).

## Out of scope

**In-place import of an existing `juanfont/headscale` deployment → RavenScale.**
No Phase-0 deployments exist, so there are no legacy rows to backfill or IPs to
re-key (the `BackfillNodeIPs` concern from the IP-allocation research has nothing
to act on). Revisit as a fresh effort only if a real migrating customer appears.

## Consequences

- The migration surface is tiny: seed data plus the tenant columns.
- Because even self-host carries a non-null `tenant_id`, the ADR-0007 CI scoping
  guard stays meaningful on self-host.
- If Headscale-DB import is later needed, it is a new, one-way, versioned
  migration designed then — not something the current schema must anticipate.

# ADR-0009: Node MachineKey stays globally unique in Phase 1

Status: Accepted (2026-08-12) · Decides [#33](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/33) · **Supersedes design decision #8 (unique-within-Tailnet)** · Map [#25](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/25)

## Context

Design decision #8 stated node WireGuard pubkeys should be unique **within a
Tailnet**, treating a device in two Tailnets as merely "out of Phase-1 scope."
Investigation of Headscale's registration flow showed this framing is wrong:

- The official Tailscale client identifies a node by its **MachineKey alone** —
  there is no Tailnet selector in the protocol, and Tailscale owns that client
  (operating principle #3), so we cannot add one.
- The known-node **reconnect lookup runs by MachineKey in the Noise handshake,
  before any credential** (and therefore before any Tailnet) is presented.

A per-Tailnet uniqueness constraint would make that pre-credential lookup
ambiguous the moment one MachineKey exists in two Tailnets — a latent bug the
client cannot help resolve.

## Decision

**MachineKey uniqueness stays global in Phase 1.**

- Uniqueness is app-enforced (lookup-before-insert), as upstream. The constraint
  is **not** composited to `(tailnet_id, machine_key)`.
- The `tenant_id`/`tailnet_id` columns are still added (queries scope), so nothing
  about the schema blocks a future cross-Tailnet-device case.
- **Exactly one deliberate global lookup survives**: the pre-credential
  known-node MachineKey lookup in the Noise handshake. Everything downstream
  (peer lists, mapresponse, node-by-id, policy) is tenant-scoped via ADR-0007.
- **Cross-Tailnet same-device is reclassified** from "deferred" to a
  **client-fork trigger candidate** (a feature needing a client change), tracked
  on P3-1 ([#20](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/issues/20)) — not a
  Phase-1 data-model choice.

## Consequences

- The reconnect path stays simple and matches upstream; no protocol change needed.
- One physical device cannot join two Tailnets until the client-fork trigger
  fires and RavenScale owns the client; the schema already carries the columns for
  that day.
- **The wiki Architecture page decision #8 is corrected** to match this ADR
  (constraint global, not within-Tailnet).

# Architecture RavenScale keeps Headscale's Tailscale-compatible coordination protocol but rebuilds the data model as **multi-tenant from day one**. This page covers the tenancy model, the eight locked design decisions, and the dependency tree that orders the work. ## Core concepts | Term | Meaning | |------|---------| | **Org** (tenant) | The billing / isolation boundary. Owns one or more Tailnets. The `tenant_id` on every table refers to the Org. | | **Tailnet** | A single virtual network namespace: its own IP space, DNS suffix, ACL policy, nodes, and users-in-network. An Org owns ≥ 1. | | **User** | An identity that authenticates to the control plane and belongs to exactly one Org. Distinct from Org and Tailnet. | | **Node** | A registered device (WireGuard peer). Belongs to exactly one Tailnet. | | **Tenant boundary** | = Org. Isolation is **logical (row-level)** on shared infrastructure. | Org, Tailnet, and User are three distinct concepts from day one — even though the launch UI exposes exactly one Tailnet per Org. ## Tenancy data model Every tenant-scoped table carries a non-null `tenant_id` (the Org). Isolation is enforced in the application layer, not the database. ```mermaid erDiagram ORG ||--o{ TAILNET : "owns (1..*)" ORG ||--o{ USER : "has members (1..*)" TAILNET ||--o{ NODE : "contains (1..*)" TAILNET ||--|| ACL_POLICY : "one HuJSON policy" ORG { int id PK "internal numeric PK" string name } TAILNET { int id PK int tenant_id FK "-> Org, never null" string slug "immutable external handle" string ip_space "independent 100.64.0.0/10" } USER { int id PK int tenant_id FK "-> Org, never null" string identity } NODE { int id PK int tenant_id FK "-> Org, never null" int tailnet_id FK "-> Tailnet" string wg_pubkey "unique within Tailnet" string addr "from this Tailnet's /10" } ACL_POLICY { int id PK int tenant_id FK "-> Org, never null" int tailnet_id FK "-> Tailnet" string hujson "resolves only within its Tailnet" } ``` Key structural properties: - **Row-level isolation, shared schema** — not schema-per-tenant, not DB-per-tenant. Mirrors Tailscale's own shared-infra logical isolation. - **Independent IP space per Tailnet** — nodes in different Tailnets may hold identical `100.64.0.0/10` addresses; they never route to each other. Allocation keys on `(tailnet_id, addr)`. - **Cross-Tailnet isolation is structural, never an ACL rule** — separate IP space + row-level scoping means a policy bug can never open a cross-tenant path. - **`tenant_id` is never null** — self-host is simply N=1 (a default Org + Tailnet), so there is exactly one code path. ## The eight locked decisions Sourced from [`CONTEXT.md`](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/blob/main/CONTEXT.md) (design-grill session 1). Hard-to-reverse calls are also recorded as ADRs. | # | Decision | Choice | Why | Ref | |---|----------|--------|-----|-----| | 1 | **Tenant model** | Tenant = Org, owns 1..* Tailnets; row-level `tenant_id`, shared schema | Mirrors Tailscale shared-infra logical isolation; an Org layer retrofitted after data exists is a migration nightmare | [ADR-0001](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/blob/main/docs/adr/0001-tenant-model-row-level-isolation.md) | | 2 | **Isolation enforcement** | App-layer mandatory scoping via one scoped repository; CI guard fails the build on unscoped tenant-table access. **libSQL single-node** backend (ADR-0005); **no** Postgres RLS (SQLite has none) | Row-level correctness must be guaranteed in code since the DB offers no RLS | CONTEXT §2 · ADR-0005 | | 3 | **IP address space** | Independent `100.64.0.0/10` per Tailnet | Full range per tenant, no cross-tenant exhaustion; isolation by construction | [ADR-0002](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/blob/main/docs/adr/0002-per-tailnet-ip-space.md) | | 4 | **Tenant resolution** | Internal user→Org mapping stamps a trusted `tenant_id` claim at auth; nodes join via **tenant-scoped pre-auth keys** (key encodes its Tailnet). Single registration endpoint; tenant derived from credential, never the URL | Keeps the join surface single and credential-driven; external per-tenant IdP is a later additive phase | CONTEXT §4 | | 5 | **Single-tenant self-host** | No separate mode — always multi-tenant with **N=1** (default Org + Tailnet, `tenant_id` never null). Migration = create default Org+Tailnet, backfill `tenant_id` (one-way, versioned). **This IS P0-2** | Two divergent code paths can never be re-merged later; one path keeps the CI scoping guard meaningful even for self-host | [ADR-0003](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/blob/main/docs/adr/0003-single-tenant-is-n-equals-1.md) | | 6 | **Tailnet naming / MagicDNS** | Immutable **slug** at creation; MagicDNS suffix `..` (base-domain per deployment). Numeric PK internal; slug is the external handle. Rename allowed but expensive | Names bake into node configs + DNS; the slug is a stable namespace that never collides across Tailnets | [ADR-0004](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/blob/main/docs/adr/0004-tailnet-slug-magicdns.md) | | 7 | **ACL policy scope** | One HuJSON policy per Tailnet; users/groups/tags resolve only within their Tailnet; no cross-Tailnet references | Cross-Tailnet isolation stays structural, so an ACL bug can never open a cross-tenant path | CONTEXT §7 | | 8 | **Node identity** | A node registers to exactly one Tailnet; WireGuard pubkey unique **within a Tailnet**, not globally. One device in two Tailnets is out of Phase-1 scope, but the node row already carries `tenant_id` + `tailnet_id` | Doesn't block the future cross-Tailnet-device case; keeps identity scoped | CONTEXT §8 | ### Known ceilings (deliberate, revisit-when) | Ceiling | Status | Revisit when | |---------|--------|--------------| | DB-per-tenant (physical isolation) | Deferred | A compliance customer needs physical isolation, or noisy-neighbor bites | | External per-tenant IdP (OIDC/SSO) | Deferred to enterprise phase | Additive; not hard to reverse | | Cross-Tailnet devices | Deferred | Schema already carries the columns | ### Datastore choice (resolved 2026-07-28) `P0-3` (#3) is settled: **libSQL (`sqld`) single-node + WAL→S3 backup, no cluster** for Phase 0–1 ([ADR-0005](https://github.com/ravencloak-org/RavenScale/blob/main/docs/adr/0005-datastore-libsql-single-node.md)). This supersedes the brief's Postgres line. The engine is reversible (GORM dialect abstraction; Headscale supports both), so clustering (LiteFS/rqlite) or Postgres is revisited at the HA milestone (#11) with real load data. Rationale + options survey: [`RESEARCH/DATASTORE_LIBSQL_VS_POSTGRES.md`](https://github.REDACTED.md). ## Dependency tree `P0-2` (#2, the multi-tenant data model) is the root nobody can route around once real data exists. Solid arrows are hard `depends` edges; dotted arrows are the `P0-4` compat-harness merge **gate** on all Phase-2 work. ```mermaid graph TD P02["P0-2 · #2
Fork + multi-tenant data model (ROOT)"] P03["P0-3 · #3
Datastore (libSQL single-node)"] P04["P0-4 · #4
Client-compat harness"] P05["P0-5 · #5
Install / upgrade + runbook"] P01["P0-1 · #1
BSD-3 + trademark"] P11["P1-1 · #6
Multi-tenancy"] P12["P1-2 · #7
Control REST API"] P13["P1-3 · #8
Admin dashboard"] P14["P1-4 · #9
IdP group sync"] P15["P1-5 · #10
Audit logs"] P16["P1-6 · #11
HA / clustering"] P17["P1-7 · #12
k8s operator"] P21["P2-1 · #13
Signed node caps + Serve"] P22["P2-2 · #14
App Connectors"] P23["P2-3 · #15
Posture checks"] P24["P2-4 · #16
Tailnet Lock / TKA"] P25["P2-5 · #17
SSH session recording"] P26["P2-6 · #18
Flow-log pipeline"] P27["P2-7 · #19
Funnel-equivalent (optional)"] P31["P3-1 · #20
Client-fork trigger gate"] P41["P4-1 · #21
Fork tailscaled + apps"] P02 --> P04 P02 --> P11 P02 --> P12 P03 --> P16 P12 --> P13 P12 --> P17 P21 --> P24 P21 --> P25 P21 --> P26 P31 -->|trigger fires| P41 P04 -.gate.-> P21 P04 -.gate.-> P22 P04 -.gate.-> P23 P04 -.gate.-> P24 P04 -.gate.-> P25 P04 -.gate.-> P26 P04 -.gate.-> P27 ``` `P0-1`, `P0-5`, `P1-4`, `P1-5`, `P2-2`, `P2-3`, `P2-7`, and `P3-1` have no stated hard `depends`; `P2-2`/`P2-3` build on the Phase-2 capabilities work and are gated by `P0-4`. See [Roadmap](Roadmap) for the full per-phase tables.

I've now read the real structs — and this is where I owe you a straight assessment rather than a blind charge.

## Where we are

**Step 1 done + pushed** — Headscale v0.29.3 forked onto `main`, module path kept (ADR-0006), `go build ./...` green. That's real, committed progress on #2 and satisfies the "builds green" half of the AC.

## Why I'm checkpointing before step 2

The schema change is genuinely invasive, not a quick edit. From the actual code:
- `User` carries `idx_name_provider_identifier` uniqueness; `Node.GivenName` has `unique_index`; MachineKey uniqueness is app-enforced — **each must be reconsidered against tenant scope** (per ADRs 0007/0009).
- New `Tenant`+`Tailnet` types + `TenantID`/`TailnetID` on User/Node/PreAuthKey/policy + an `rs-0001-tenancy` gormigrate migration + the default-Org/Tailnet seed (ADR-0008).
- Then steps 3–7 (scoped session, per-Tailnet IP allocator, registration stamping, CI guard) each **change behavior** and must keep Headscale's large existing test suite green.

That's hundreds of lines across ~10 files where a confident-wrong edit ships a latent isolation bug — the exact thing the ADRs exist to prevent. It shouldn't be one blind blast.

## Two ways to proceed

**A — Delegate the data-model build to a coding agent** (Forge or Engineer) with the four ADRs + research branches as the spec, test-suite-gated. Best fit for a 10-file invasive change.

**B — Increment with me now**, smallest safe steps: start with the additive schema scaffold (new `Tenant`/`Tailnet` types + `rs-0001` migration + nullable-default `tenant_id` columns) that builds green and breaks nothing, then tackle the behavioral steps one session each, running the relevant package tests each time.

I recommend **B** for control (each increment verified), or **A** if you want it driven to done in one delegated push. Which?

=== schema.sql ===
-- This file is the representation of the SQLite schema of Headscale.
-- It is the "source of truth" and is used to validate any migrations
-- that are run against the database to ensure it ends in the expected state.

CREATE TABLE migrations(id text,PRIMARY KEY(id));

CREATE TABLE users(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  name text,
  display_name text,
  email text,
  provider_identifier text,
  provider text,
  profile_pic_url text,

  created_at datetime,
  updated_at datetime,
  deleted_at datetime
);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_deleted_at ON users(deleted_at);


-- The following three UNIQUE indexes work together to enforce the user identity model:
--
-- 1. Users can be either local (provider_identifier is NULL) or from external providers (provider_identifier set)
-- 2. Each external provider identifier must be unique across the system
-- 3. Local usernames must be unique among local users
-- 4. The same username can exist across different providers with different identifiers
--
-- Examples:
-- - Can create local user "alice" (provider_identifier=NULL)
-- - Can create external user "alice" with GitHub (name="alice", provider_identifier="alice_github")
-- - Can create external user "alice" with Google (name="alice", provider_identifier="alice_google")
-- - Cannot create another local user "alice" (blocked by idx_name_no_provider_identifier)
-- - Cannot create another user with provider_identifier="alice_github" (blocked by idx_provider_identifier)
-- - Cannot create user "bob" with provider_identifier="alice_github" (blocked by idx_name_provider_identifier)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_provider_identifier ON users(provider_identifier) WHERE provider_identifier IS NOT NULL;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_name_provider_identifier ON users(name, provider_identifier);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_name_no_provider_identifier ON users(name) WHERE provider_identifier IS NULL;

CREATE TABLE pre_auth_keys(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  key text,
  prefix text,
  hash blob,
  user_id integer,
  reusable numeric,
  ephemeral numeric DEFAULT false,
  used numeric DEFAULT false,
  tags text,
  expiration datetime,

  created_at datetime,

  CONSTRAINT fk_pre_auth_keys_user FOREIGN KEY(user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_pre_auth_keys_prefix ON pre_auth_keys(prefix) WHERE prefix IS NOT NULL AND prefix != '';

CREATE TABLE api_keys(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  prefix text,
  hash blob,
  expiration datetime,
  last_seen datetime,

  created_at datetime
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_api_keys_prefix ON api_keys(prefix);

CREATE TABLE nodes(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  machine_key text,
  node_key text,
  disco_key text,

  endpoints text,
  host_info text,
  ipv4 text,
  ipv6 text,
  hostname text,
  given_name varchar(63),
  -- user_id is NULL for tagged nodes (owned by tags, not a user).
  -- Only set for user-owned nodes (no tags).
  user_id integer,
  register_method text,
  tags text,
  auth_key_id integer,
  last_seen datetime,
  expiry datetime,
  approved_routes text,

  created_at datetime,
  updated_at datetime,
  deleted_at datetime,

  CONSTRAINT fk_nodes_user FOREIGN KEY(user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT fk_nodes_auth_key FOREIGN KEY(auth_key_id) REFERENCES pre_auth_keys(id)
);

CREATE TABLE policies(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  data text,

  created_at datetime,
  updated_at datetime,
  deleted_at datetime
);
CREATE INDEX idx_policies_deleted_at ON policies(deleted_at);

CREATE TABLE database_versions(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  version text NOT NULL,
  updated_at datetime
);

-- This file is the representation of the SQLite schema of Headscale.
-- It is the "source of truth" and is used to validate any migrations
-- that are run against the database to ensure it ends in the expected state.

CREATE TABLE migrations(id text,PRIMARY KEY(id));

-- RavenScale multi-tenancy (ADR-0001): Tenant = Org (isolation boundary),
-- owns 1..* Tailnets. Every tenant-scoped table carries a non-null tenant_id
-- (the Org) and, where it lives in a network namespace, a tailnet_id.
CREATE TABLE tenants(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  name text,

  created_at datetime,
  updated_at datetime,
  deleted_at datetime
);
CREATE INDEX idx_tenants_deleted_at ON tenants(deleted_at);

CREATE TABLE tailnets(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  tenant_id integer NOT NULL,
  slug text,
  name text,

  created_at datetime,
  updated_at datetime,
  deleted_at datetime
);
CREATE INDEX idx_tailnets_deleted_at ON tailnets(deleted_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_tailnets_tenant_id ON tailnets(tenant_id);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_tailnets_slug ON tailnets(slug);

CREATE TABLE users(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  tenant_id integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  name text,
  display_name text,
  email text,
  provider_identifier text,
  provider text,
  profile_pic_url text,

  created_at datetime,
  updated_at datetime,
  deleted_at datetime
);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_deleted_at ON users(deleted_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_tenant_id ON users(tenant_id);


-- The following three UNIQUE indexes work together to enforce the user identity model:
--
-- 1. Users can be either local (provider_identifier is NULL) or from external providers (provider_identifier set)
-- 2. Each external provider identifier must be unique across the system
-- 3. Local usernames must be unique among local users
-- 4. The same username can exist across different providers with different identifiers
--
-- Examples:
-- - Can create local user "alice" (provider_identifier=NULL)
-- - Can create external user "alice" with GitHub (name="alice", provider_identifier="alice_github")
-- - Can create external user "alice" with Google (name="alice", provider_identifier="alice_google")
-- - Cannot create another local user "alice" (blocked by idx_name_no_provider_identifier)
-- - Cannot create another user with provider_identifier="alice_github" (blocked by idx_provider_identifier)
-- - Cannot create user "bob" with provider_identifier="alice_github" (blocked by idx_name_provider_identifier)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_provider_identifier ON users(provider_identifier) WHERE provider_identifier IS NOT NULL;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_name_provider_identifier ON users(name, provider_identifier);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_name_no_provider_identifier ON users(name) WHERE provider_identifier IS NULL;

CREATE TABLE pre_auth_keys(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  tenant_id integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  tailnet_id integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  key text,
  prefix text,
  hash blob,
  user_id integer,
  reusable numeric,
  ephemeral numeric DEFAULT false,
  used numeric DEFAULT false,
  tags text,
  expiration datetime,

  created_at datetime,

  CONSTRAINT fk_pre_auth_keys_user FOREIGN KEY(user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_pre_auth_keys_prefix ON pre_auth_keys(prefix) WHERE prefix IS NOT NULL AND prefix != '';
CREATE INDEX idx_pre_auth_keys_tenant_id ON pre_auth_keys(tenant_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_pre_auth_keys_tailnet_id ON pre_auth_keys(tailnet_id);

CREATE TABLE api_keys(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  prefix text,
  hash blob,
  expiration datetime,
  last_seen datetime,

  created_at datetime
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_api_keys_prefix ON api_keys(prefix);

CREATE TABLE nodes(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  tenant_id integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  tailnet_id integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  machine_key text,
  node_key text,
  disco_key text,

  endpoints text,
  host_info text,
  ipv4 text,
  ipv6 text,
  hostname text,
  given_name varchar(63),
  -- user_id is NULL for tagged nodes (owned by tags, not a user).
  -- Only set for user-owned nodes (no tags).
  user_id integer,
  register_method text,
  tags text,
  auth_key_id integer,
  last_seen datetime,
  expiry datetime,
  approved_routes text,

  created_at datetime,
  updated_at datetime,
  deleted_at datetime,

  CONSTRAINT fk_nodes_user FOREIGN KEY(user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT fk_nodes_auth_key FOREIGN KEY(auth_key_id) REFERENCES pre_auth_keys(id)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_nodes_tenant_id ON nodes(tenant_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_nodes_tailnet_id ON nodes(tailnet_id);

CREATE TABLE policies(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  tenant_id integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  tailnet_id integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  data text,

  created_at datetime,
  updated_at datetime,
  deleted_at datetime
);
CREATE INDEX idx_policies_deleted_at ON policies(deleted_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_policies_tenant_id ON policies(tenant_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_policies_tailnet_id ON policies(tailnet_id);

CREATE TABLE database_versions(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY,
  version text NOT NULL,
  updated_at datetime
);

content.text:
`TestConstraints` (fresh boot) = **`ok`**. That's the decisive result.

## Where step 2 actually stands

- **Build green.** `go build ./...` = 0.
- **Fresh-install path green** — `TestConstraints` passes; the dump shows `INSERT INTO users (... tenant_id ...) VALUES (... 1 ...)` — tenant columns, defaults, tenant/tailnet tables, seed all working on a new DB.
- **2 tests fail:** `TestSQLiteAllTestdataMigrations` + `TestSQLiteMigrationAndDataValidation`. Both **replay ancient Headscale DB dumps forward** through the full historical migration chain. Adding `tenant_id` to the shared structs makes Headscale's old typed-model migrations (`ListUsers`/`tx.Save`, both pre- and post-table-recreation) reference a column that doesn't exist at that point in history.

## The key insight

A **greenfield RavenScale DB never replays those historical migrations** — it boots via `InitSchema` (all migrations marked applied, skipped), tenancy present in the first schema it ever sees. The only way to hit that replay path is **importing an existing `juanfont/headscale` deployment** — which **ADR-0008 explicitly ruled out of scope.**

So those two failing tests validate out-of-scope behavior.

## Decision needed

**A — Support old-dump replay anyway.** Insert two idempotent raw-`ALTER` migrations (one before the first typed migration, one after the v0.27 table-recreation) so `tenant_id` exists continuously. ~40 lines, no upstream-body edits, keeps all tests green — but builds machinery for a path ADR-0008 says we don't need.

**B — Apply ADR-0008.** Skip the two dump-replay tests with a documented `t.Skip("ADR-0008: Headscale-DB import out of scope")`. Zero new machinery; honors the decision. Risk: a future upstream merge that changes those tests needs a re-look.

I recommend **B** — it's literally what ADR-0008 decided, and A is effort spent on ruled-out scope. Which?

-- This file is the representation of the SQLite schema of Headscale.
-- It is the "source of truth" and is used to validate any migrations
-- that are run against the database to ensure it ends in the expected state.

CREATE TABLE migrations(id text,PRIMARY KEY(id));

-- RavenScale multi-tenancy (ADR-0001): Tenant = Org (isolation boundary),
-- owns 1..* Tailnets. Every tenant-scoped table carries a non-null tenant_id
-- (the Org) and, where it lives in a network namespace, a tailnet_id.
CREATE TABLE tenants(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  name text,

  created_at datetime,
  updated_at datetime,
  deleted_at datetime
);
CREATE INDEX `idx_tenants_deleted_at` ON `tenants`(`deleted_at`);

CREATE TABLE tailnets(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  tenant_id integer NOT NULL,
  slug text,
  name text,

  created_at datetime,
  updated_at datetime,
  deleted_at datetime
);
CREATE INDEX `idx_tailnets_deleted_at` ON `tailnets`(`deleted_at`);
CREATE INDEX `idx_tailnets_tenant_id` ON `tailnets`(`tenant_id`);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX `idx_tailnets_slug` ON `tailnets`(`slug`);

CREATE TABLE users(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  tenant_id integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  name text,
  display_name text,
  email text,
  provider_identifier text,
  provider text,
  profile_pic_url text,

  created_at datetime,
  updated_at datetime,
  deleted_at datetime
);
CREATE INDEX idx_users_deleted_at ON users(deleted_at);
CREATE INDEX `idx_users_tenant_id` ON `users`(`tenant_id`);


-- The following three UNIQUE indexes work together to enforce the user identity model:
--
-- 1. Users can be either local (provider_identifier is NULL) or from external providers (provider_identifier set)
-- 2. Each external provider identifier must be unique across the system
-- 3. Local usernames must be unique among local users
-- 4. The same username can exist across different providers with different identifiers
--
-- Examples:
-- - Can create local user "alice" (provider_identifier=NULL)
-- - Can create external user "alice" with GitHub (name="alice", provider_identifier="alice_github")
-- - Can create external user "alice" with Google (name="alice", provider_identifier="alice_google")
-- - Cannot create another local user "alice" (blocked by idx_name_no_provider_identifier)
-- - Cannot create another user with provider_identifier="alice_github" (blocked by idx_provider_identifier)
-- - Cannot create user "bob" with provider_identifier="alice_github" (blocked by idx_name_provider_identifier)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_provider_identifier ON users(provider_identifier) WHERE provider_identifier IS NOT NULL;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_name_provider_identifier ON users(name, provider_identifier);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_name_no_provider_identifier ON users(name) WHERE provider_identifier IS NULL;

CREATE TABLE pre_auth_keys(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  tenant_id integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  tailnet_id integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  key text,
  prefix text,
  hash blob,
  user_id integer,
  reusable numeric,
  ephemeral numeric DEFAULT false,
  used numeric DEFAULT false,
  tags text,
  expiration datetime,

  created_at datetime,

  CONSTRAINT fk_pre_auth_keys_user FOREIGN KEY(user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_pre_auth_keys_prefix ON pre_auth_keys(prefix) WHERE prefix IS NOT NULL AND prefix != '';
CREATE INDEX `idx_pre_auth_keys_tenant_id` ON `pre_auth_keys`(`tenant_id`);
CREATE INDEX `idx_pre_auth_keys_tailnet_id` ON `pre_auth_keys`(`tailnet_id`);

CREATE TABLE api_keys(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  prefix text,
  hash blob,
  expiration datetime,
  last_seen datetime,

  created_at datetime
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_api_keys_prefix ON api_keys(prefix);

CREATE TABLE nodes(
  id integer PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  tenant_id integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  tailnet_id integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  machine_key text,
  node_key text,
  disco_key text,

  endpoints text,
  host_info text,
  ipv4 text,
  ipv6 text,
  hostname text,
  given_name varchar(63),
  -- user_id is NULL for tagged nodes (owned by tags, not a user).
  -- Only set for user-owned nodes (no tags).
  user_id integer,
  register_method text,
  tags text,
  auth_key_id integer,
  last_seen datetime,
  expiry datetime,
  approved_routes text,

  created_at datetime,
  updated_at datetime,
  deleted_at datetime,

  CONSTRAINT fk_nodes_user FOREIGN KEY(user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT fk_nodes_auth_key FOREIGN KEY(auth_key_id) REFERENCES pre_auth_keys(id)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
- /figma-use-figjam — for FigJam-specific use_f… [truncated]

## claude.ai Linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

## context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

## tokensave
tokensave is a code-graph MCP server. Start with tokensave_context for any code exploration task — it returns relevant symbols, relationships, and code snippets for a natural-language query. Use tokensave_search to find specific symbols by name. Discovery and analysis tools are read-only and safe to call in parallel. Edit and session-memory tools can mutate local project state and declare readOnlyHint=false. When a tool result contains a `tokensave_metrics:` line, report the savings to the user (e.g. 'TokenSave\'d ~N tokens').

PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE — level: full

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you

# Prototype

A prototype is **throwaway code that answers a question**. The question decides the shape.

## Pick a branch

Identify which question is being answered — from the user's prompt, the surrounding code, or by asking if the user is around:

- **"Does this logic / state model feel right?"** → [LOGIC.md](LOGIC.md). Build a single shareable HTML file — free-play buttons plus tabbed guided walkthroughs — that pushes the state machine through cases that are hard to reason about on paper, and that a non-developer can drive.
- **"What should this look like?"** → [UI.md](UI.md). Generate several radically different UI variations on a single route, switchable via a URL search param and a floating bottom bar.

The two branches produce very different artifacts — getting this wrong wastes the whole prototype. If the question is genuinely ambiguous and the user isn't reachable, default to whichever branch better matches the surrounding code (a backend module → logic; a page or component → UI) and state the assumption at the top of the prototype.

## Rules that apply to both

1. **Throwaway from day one, and clearly marked as such.** Locate the prototype code close to where it will actually be used (next to the module or page it's prototyping for) so context is obvious — but name it so a casual reader can see it's a prototype, not production. For throwaway UI routes, obey whatever routing convention the project already uses; don't invent a new top-level structure.
2. **Trivial to run.** A UI prototype starts from one command in the project's task runner — `pnpm <name>`, `python <path>`, `bun <path>`, etc. A logic demo is a single HTML file the user double-clicks. Either way, no thinking required to start it.
3. **No persistence by default.** State lives in memory. Persistence is the thing the prototype is _checking_, not something it should depend on. If the question explicitly involves a database, hit a scratch DB or a local file with a clear "PROTOTYPE — wipe me" name.
4. **Skip the polish.** No tests, no error handling beyond what makes the prototype _runnable_, no abstractions. The point is to learn something fast.
5. **Surface the state.** After every action (logic) or on every variant switch (UI), print or render the full relevant state so the user can see what changed.
6. **Capture it when done.** Fold any validated decision into the real code, then capture the prototype itself as a **primary source**: commit it to a throwaway branch, out of main, and leave a context pointer to that branch on the implementation issue. Capture the answer too — the verdict and the question it settled — in the issue or a commit. The main branch keeps only the validated decision.

content.content:
# RavenScale — CONTEXT

Multi-tenant SaaS control plane built on Headscale (open-source Tailscale coordination server). This file captures resolved terminology and foundational design decisions from the design-grill sessions. Hard-to-reverse calls are recorded as ADRs under `docs/adr/`.

## Terminology (nailed)

| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **Org** (tenant) | The billing/isolation boundary. Owns one or more Tailnets. The `tenant_id` on every table refers to the Org. |
| **Tailnet** | A single virtual network namespace: its own IP space, DNS suffix, ACL policy, nodes, and users-in-network. An Org owns ≥1. |
| **User** | An identity that authenticates to the control plane and belongs to exactly one Org. Distinct concept from Org and Tailnet. |
| **Node** | A registered device (WireGuard peer). Belongs to exactly one Tailnet. |
| **Tenant boundary** | = Org. Isolation is logical (row-level), on shared infrastructure. |

Org / Tailnet / User are three distinct concepts from day one, even though the launch UI exposes exactly one Tailnet per Org.

## Resolved decisions (design grill, session 1 — Q1–Q8)

1. **Tenant model** — Tenant = Org, owns one-or-more Tailnets. Row-level `tenant_id`, shared schema. Mirrors Tailscale's shared-infra logical isolation. → ADR-0001
2. **Isolation enforcement** — App-layer mandatory scoping: all tenant-table access routes through one scoped repository; a CI guard fails the build on any unscoped access to a tenant table. SQLite is the backend (Turso/libSQL for horizontal scale later — same wire, still no RLS, so app-layer stays primary). Postgres RLS is *not* used (SQLite has none).
3. **IP address space** — Per-Tailnet independent `100.64.0.0/10`. Nodes in different Tailnets may hold identical addresses; they never route to each other. → ADR-0002
4. **Tenant resolution** — Internal user→Org mapping stamps a trusted `tenant_id` claim at auth. Nodes join via **tenant-scoped pre-auth keys** (the key encodes its Tailnet); the registration endpoint stays single, tenant is derived from the credential, never the URL. External per-tenant IdP is a later, additive phase.
5. **Single-tenant self-host** — No separate mode. Always multi-tenant with **N=1**: a default Org + Tailnet, `tenant_id` never null. Migration of existing Headscale installs = create the default Org+Tailnet and backfill `tenant_id` on every row (one-way, versioned). This IS P0-2. → ADR-0003
6. **Tailnet naming / MagicDNS** — Each Tailnet gets an **immutable slug** at creation; MagicDNS suffix is `<host>.<tailnet-slug>.<base-domain>`, base-domain per deployment. Numeric PK stays internal; the slug is the external handle. Rename is allowed but expensive (breaks DNS) and treated as a rare op. → ADR-0004
7. **ACL policy scope** — One HuJSON ACL policy per Tailnet. Users/groups/tags resolve only within their Tailnet; no cross-Tailnet references. Cross-Tailnet isolation is *structural* (separate IP space + row-level scoping), never expressed as an ACL rule — so a policy bug can never open a cross-tenant path.
8. **Node identity** — A node registers to exactly one Tailnet; its WireGuard pubkey is unique **within a Tailnet**, not globally. One device in two Tailnets is out of scope for Phase 1, but the node row already carries `tenant_id` + `tailnet_id`, so it is not blocked later.

## Known ceilings (deliberate, revisit-when)

- **DB-per-tenant** — deferred; revisit only if a customer needs physical isolation for compliance, or noisy-neighbor bites. Row-level keeps HA / backup-restore / k8s-operator simple.
- **External per-tenant IdP (OIDC/SSO)** — deferred to enterprise phase; additive, not hard to reverse.
- **Cross-Tailnet devices** — deferred; schema already carries the columns.

## Sources

Design grill session 1, Buzz channel `ravenscale-grill` (#d4978296-701f-4425-a5d5-d440e572ec93), 2026-07-27. Tailscale architecture claims are from public docs/architecture knowledge, not a live doc pull.

1. **Tenant model** — Tenant = Org, owns one-or-more Tailnets. Row-level `tenant_id`, shared schema. Mirrors Tailscale's shared-infra logical isolation. → ADR-0001
2. **Isolation enforcement** — App-layer mandatory scoping: all tenant-table access routes through one scoped repository; a CI guard fails the build on any unscoped access to a tenant table. SQLite is the backend (Turso/libSQL for horizontal scale later — same wire, still no RLS, so app-layer stays primary). Postgres RLS is *not* used (SQLite has none).
3. **IP address space** — Per-Tailnet independent `100.64.0.0/10`. Nodes in different Tailnets may hold identical addresses; they never route to each other. → ADR-0002
4. **Tenant resolution** — Internal user→Org mapping stamps a trusted `tenant_id` claim at auth. Nodes join via **tenant-scoped pre-auth keys** (the key encodes its Tailnet); the registration endpoint stays single, tenant is derived from the credential, never the URL. External per-tenant IdP is a later, additive phase.
5. **Single-tenant self-host** — No separate mode. Always multi-tenant with **N=1**: a default Org + Tailnet, `tenant_id` never null. Migration of existing Headscale installs = create the default Org+Tailnet and backfill `tenant_id` on every row (one-way, versioned). This IS P0-2. → ADR-0003
6. **Tailnet naming / MagicDNS** — Each Tailnet gets an **immutable slug** at creation; MagicDNS suffix is `<host>.<tailnet-slug>.<base-domain>`, base-domain per deployment. Numeric PK stays internal; the slug is the external handle. Rename is allowed but expensive (breaks DNS) and treated as a rare op. → ADR-0004
7. **ACL policy scope** — One HuJSON ACL policy per Tailnet. Users/groups/tags resolve only within their Tailnet; no cross-Tailnet references. Cross-Tailnet isolation is *structural* (separate IP space + row-level scoping), never expressed as an ACL rule — so a policy bug can never open a cross-tenant path.
8. **Node identity** — A node registers to exactly one Tailnet; its WireGuard pubkey is unique **within a Tailnet**, not globally. One device in two Tailnets is out of scope for Phase 1, but the node row already carries `tenant_id` + `tailnet_id`, so it is not blocked later.

## Known ceilings (deliberate, revisit-when)

- **DB-per-tenant** — deferred; revisit only if a customer needs physical isolation for compliance, or noisy-neighbor bites. Row-level keeps HA / backup-restore / k8s-operator simple.
- **External per-tenant IdP (OIDC/SSO)** — deferred to enterprise phase; additive, not hard to reverse.
- **Cross-Tailnet devices** — deferred; schema already carries the columns.

## Sources

Design grill session 1, Buzz channel `ravenscale-grill` (#d4978296-701f-4425-a5d5-d440e572ec93), 2026-07-27. Tailscale architecture claims are from public docs/architecture knowledge, not a live doc pull.

Here is the re-pitch. Simple sentences. Domain terms from `CONTEXT.md`.

## Where we are

We build **RavenScale**. It is a multi-tenant control plane on Headscale. One **Org** is the tenant boundary. One Org owns one or more **Tailnets**. A **User** belongs to one Org. A **Node** belongs to one Tailnet.

We do the work in small steps. We finished **Step 2**. Step 2 added the `tenant_id` and `tailnet_id` columns to the tables. It also added the default Org and default Tailnet for the N=1 self-host case. Step 2 is committed and pushed. The tests pass.

## What the prototype is for

**Step 3** is the next step. Step 3 builds the **scoped repository** from decision 2 in `CONTEXT.md`. This is the one path that all access to a tenant table must go through.

I did not write Step 3 yet. First I built a **throwaway model** of it. The model is one HTML file. You open it in a browser. It does not touch the database. It only shows the rules.

The rules are these:

1. **A request carries an Org.** The scoped repository reads the Org from the request. Then it adds `WHERE tenant_id = <that Org>` to every query.
2. **No Org means refuse.** If the request has no Org, the repository returns an error. It does not return the rows of all Orgs. This is the safe default.
3. **One Org cannot touch another Org's row.** An update or a delete on a foreign row changes zero rows.
4. **An admin can opt out.** The admin calls `WithAllTenants`. Then the repository does not add the Org filter. This path is rare and easy to find in the code.
5. **Raw SQL escapes the rules.** A raw query does not go through the repository. So it sees all rows. This is a known hole. A later step (Step 7) adds a **CI guard**. The guard fails the build on raw SQL and on cross-table joins.

## What I need from you

Open the file. Click the buttons. Run the 5 walkthroughs at the bottom.

Check **one** decision: when the admin uses `WithAllTenants` **and** creates a new row, my model **refuses**. The reason is that the model cannot know which Org to write on the new row. Tell me if this rule is correct.

When you approve the rules, I write the real Step 3 to match them.

content.text:
Let me strip it all the way down.

## The problem

RavenScale has many customers (Orgs) sharing **one database**. Alice's company and Bob's company both have rows in the same `users` table, the same `nodes` table. Each row has a `tenant_id` saying which Org owns it.

The danger: if any query forgets `WHERE tenant_id = mine`, Alice sees Bob's data. That is a data leak. Fatal for a SaaS.

## The fix (Step 3)

Instead of trusting every query to remember the filter, we build **one gate** that adds `WHERE tenant_id = ...` automatically. Every read/write goes through the gate. Forgetting is impossible.

That gate is the thing Step 3 builds. I have not built it yet.

## What "it" is

"It" = a **fake, clickable demo of that gate**, in a web page. Not real code. Not the database. Just a drawing of the rules that come alive when you click.

Why build a fake first: the gate has tricky corner cases (no Org? admin override? raw SQL?). Cheaper to click through them on a toy than to write the real Go code, discover a rule is wrong, and rewrite it.

You click "Query as Org 1" → the page shows only Org 1's rows, dims the rest. You click "no Org" → it refuses. That is the whole thing. It shows me you agree the rules are right, **then** I write the real gate to match.

Want me to just skip the demo and write the real Step 3? The demo is optional — it only exists to catch a wrong rule early.
